A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GenExam. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, including the benchmark taxonomy, prompts, evaluation framework, tables and figures. Changes in formatting and placement can be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations, expert ratings and evaluator ablations in Tables 2–4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds results for newer generators, additional evaluators and a human-alignment study covering five more generators.

M1.justification: The proposed curation and evaluation framework remains unchanged: GPT-5-assisted annotation, customized scoring questions, reference-image judging, and strict and relaxed scores. Text-reference alternatives are evaluator ablations. V3's expanded description of accompanying source text does not establish a method change; v1's annotation template already accepts related text.

E1.justification: The ten subjects, source datasets, four-level taxonomy, image types and exam-generation tasks are retained, as are GenExam-Full and GenExam-Mini. Additional human-rated outputs extend validation within existing task coverage. History and music examples exchange main-text and appendix placement rather than introducing new domains.

E2.justification: Table 2 introduces Nano Banana Pro, GPT-Image-1.5, Seedream 4.5, FLUX.2 max/dev and Qwen-Image-2512 while removing several earlier comparators. Table 4 adds Gemini-3-Flash and Qwen3-VL thinking/instruct evaluators. Tables 8–9 also remove Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large and BLIP3o-NEXT-GRPO-Text-3B from those comparisons, although they remain elsewhere.

E3.justification: The main scoring rules, weights and low-reasoning GPT-5 setting are retained. Added protocols include 500 additional human-alignment samples and text-only or image-plus-text reference conditions. Figure 11 also revises one economics scoring question from zero wage to a negative value, -H. These extend or locally revise evaluation without replacing its overall design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's evaluator and reasoning-effort ablations, v3 tests whether GPT-5-generated captions can replace or supplement reference images. Table 5 examines human alignment across five additional generators, addressing generalization beyond v1's GPT-Image-1 outputs. Error analysis and qualitative evidence are also revised around newer generators.

E5.justification: New Table 5 reports standard deviations alongside MAE for four evaluation dimensions and interprets them as evidence of inter-rater reliability. V1 reports MAE, correlations and p-values without this variability reporting. The standard-deviation calculation is not explained precisely, and no added seed or repeated-run protocol is specified.

E6.justification: V1's leading Table 2 result is GPT-Image-1 at 12.1 strict and 62.6 relaxed; those values remain in v3. Newly evaluated Nano Banana Pro scores 72.7/93.7 and GPT-Image-1.5 scores 43.2/82.3, substantially changing the ranking. Numerous appendix results and qualitative outputs are added or replaced, including new evaluator and human-alignment findings.

T1.justification: The strict and relaxed scoring definitions and weights are retained. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs. The new reference-modality explanations and validation results do not introduce formal mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes that even the strongest models score below 15% strictly. V3 acknowledges strong performance from Nano Banana Pro and GPT-Image-1.5 and reframes the principal empirical takeaway around remaining difficulty and the open/closed-source gap. This substantially narrows the universal-failure claim, while retaining the benchmark and evaluation-framework contributions.

C2.justification: V3 develops an explanation emphasizing failures to translate knowledge into readable visual outputs, adds spatial-fidelity arguments for image references, and claims broader metric generalizability. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit limitations concerning incomplete disciplinary coverage and dependence on judges' knowledge, including possible bias and niche-domain errors.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly explains how webpage descriptions, lecture notes and question-answer text support annotation. V3 identifies GPT-5 as the caption generator for reference ablations and adds evaluator cost/time information. However, it omits v1's exact gpt-5-2025-08-07 evaluator identifier. The annotation/evaluation templates and benchmark/code access link remain available.

R1.justification: V3 adds references for newer models, including Nano Banana Pro, GPT-Image-1.5, FLUX.2 and Gemini-3-Flash, while trimming peripheral understanding and reasoning literature. It explicitly relates strict scoring to RISEBench. The central positioning against concept-illustration and understanding benchmarks remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Related work is condensed, detailed data curation moves into Appendix B, and the results and error-analysis prose are revised. Ethics and limitations sections disappear. These are meaningful but bounded editorial and structural changes; much of the introduction, scoring explanation, taxonomy and prompt text remains closely matched.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one to two columns. Figure 1 is simplified, qualitative model panels are replaced and redistributed, and the curation diagram moves to the appendix with additional source-text information. V3 adds a human-alignment table and combines previously separate Mini and difficulty tables. These substantially change the visual presentation beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: Validation on 500 additional outputs and the new evaluator/reference ablations address v1's limited human-alignment evidence. However, v3 removes substantive limitations and introduces reporting conflicts: Gemini's Spearman correlation is 0.8200 in Table 3 versus 0.8300 in Table 4, and Figure 6 assigns strict score 1 alongside semantic correctness 0.58. The PDFs do not establish whether these are isolated transcription errors or broader scoring problems, leaving the net quality effect uncertain.
